stops.name: Commons Beach
stops.teaser: The pier where a lumber baron's railroad met the lake.
stops.map: Commons Beach Park, 400 North Lake Blvd, Tahoe City, CA
stops.clue: Walk to the lakefront park in Tahoe City. Look for the historical markers near the bike path and the old pier area.

now.head: Today
now.label: The waterfront today
now.line: The Tahoe City waterfront, with its marina and pier.

story: After the Comstock mines declined in the 1890s, lumber baron Duane L. Bliss turned from timber to tourism. He took his Glenbrook operation apart and shipped its buildings across the lake by barge. At Tahoe City he built a railroad line to the pier at Commons Beach, began the grand Tahoe Tavern hotel and built the two-story Tahoe Mercantile on the pier.

He formed the Lake Tahoe Railway and Transportation Company. By 1902 passenger cars ran along 15 miles of narrow gauge track from Truckee to a trestle pier at Tahoe City. About 25 years later the Linnard Steamship Company and Southern Pacific replaced it with standard gauge track, and Snowball Specials carried visitors to winter sports. During World War II the tracks were taken up and the rails recycled.

Not everyone liked it. Many people opposed the use of public lands, and lumberman Walter Bickford won a lawsuit against Bliss, but it did not stop the development. Bliss died in 1907 and his son William took over. A mysterious fire in 1937 destroyed the Mercantile, the post office and the Cedar Log Saloon. The Tahoe Tavern was torn down in 1964.
stops.fact: Snowball Specials carried winter sports fans on this railway.
stops.disputed: The marker says the standard gauge change came about 25 years after 1902, so the exact year is not given.

claims.t: A narrow gauge railway reached the Tahoe City pier by 1902.
claims.why: A historical marker says passenger cars ran 15 miles from Truckee by 1902.

claims.t: The Truckee-to-Tahoe City railway still runs today.
claims.why: The tracks were dismantled during World War II.

stops.name: Lake Tahoe Dam
stops.teaser: A small dam that controls a giant lake.
stops.map: Lake Tahoe Dam, Tahoe City, CA
stops.clue: Follow the water to where it leaves the lake. A low concrete dam with a row of gates holds back Lake Tahoe, and a walkway runs along the top.
stops.safety: Tahoe City sidewalks are busy with cars, bikes and visitors. Cross only at marked crossings. Stay behind railings near the water. The river runs fast and cold, so never climb on rocks or walls, and keep your hands and feet out of the outlet.
stops.field: Field notes pending: the viewing areas have not been checked on foot yet.

now.head: Today
now.label: The dam today
now.line: A National Register of Historic Places listing since March 25, 1981. Photo taken in 2012.

story: A small dam of lumber and rock was built at the outlet in 1870. Sources disagree on who built it, so we list both names below.
The present concrete dam was built between 1909 and 1913 to store irrigation water for the Newlands Project, which waters about 55,000 acres of farmland in Nevada.
It controls the top six feet of the lake and can raise it by up to 10.1 feet. The federal government bought it in 1915 for $139,500.
stops.fact: The dam is only 18.2 feet high and 109 feet long, yet it regulates the top six feet of a lake 22 miles long.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia says the Donner Lumber and Boom Company got the right to build the 1870 dam. The state historical marker says Colonel A. W. Von Schmidt built the first outlet works in 1870. The sources do not agree on who.

claims.t: The Lake Tahoe Dam was finished in 1913.
claims.why: The historical marker and Wikipedia agree on 1913.

claims.t: The dam can raise Lake Tahoe by more than 30 feet.
claims.why: It regulates the top six feet and can raise the lake up to 10.1 feet.

stops.name: Gatekeeper's Museum
stops.teaser: A log cabin for the person who kept the lake's gates.
stops.clue: Beside the dam, in a small park, look for a log cabin built for the person who opened and closed the gates. Today it is a museum.
stops.safety: Tahoe City sidewalks are busy with cars, bikes and visitors. Cross only at marked crossings. Stay behind railings near the water. The river runs fast and cold, so never climb on rocks or walls, and keep your hands and feet out of the outlet. The museum is open seasonally. You do not need to go inside.

story: The gatekeeper's job was to open and close the dam gates and keep the lake and river at the right levels. A cabin went up in 1910 so the gatekeeper could live beside the gates.
In 1910 and 1911 the Tahoe Water War between lakeshore owners and downstream river users was settled. Measuring the snow's water content let people predict river and lake levels.
The original cabin burned in 1978. The present one was finished in 1981 and is a museum with local history exhibits and a collection of Native baskets.
stops.fact: The site became California Registered Historical Landmark No. 797 on September 16, 1964.

claims.t: The cabin you see today is the original from 1910.
claims.why: The original burned in 1978. The present cabin was completed in 1981.

claims.t: The museum in the rebuilt cabin holds a collection of Native baskets.
claims.why: The historical marker page describes the cabin as housing local history exhibits and a Native basket collection.

now.head: Today
now.label: A museum
now.line: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places on August 24, 1979. Photo taken in 2012.

story: Robert Montgomery Watson came to Tahoe City in 1875 and became its first constable. In 1908 he built a log cabin for his son and daughter-in-law. They moved in during 1909.
From 1947 until 1976 the family leased it to E. P. and Fern Hunt, who ran it as a summer gift shop.
The Tahoe City Public Utility District and the North Lake Tahoe Historical Society bought it in 1979. Today it is a museum and gift shop, restored in 2024 and 2025.
stops.fact: The cabin stands at 560 N. Lake Blvd and is owned by the North Lake Tahoe Historical Society.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia calls it the only historic log cabin in the Tahoe City area, and one local magazine says it was submitted as Tahoe's oldest home. Those are claims from the sources, not something we could check.

claims.why: Wikipedia and Tahoe Magazine both give 1908.

claims.t: Watson Cabin is the oldest home in all of Tahoe.
claims.why: One magazine says it was submitted as Tahoe's oldest home, but we found no source that proves it.

sources.t: Tahoe Magazine: The history and future of Watson Cabin

mission: Find four landmarks where the Truckee River leaves Lake Tahoe. At each one, check in to earn its badge, unlock its story, and collect a Time Card. Do them in any order. Everything stays on this phone.
afterDone: All four badges earned. You know where the Truckee River begins.
safetyNote: • All four stops are in Tahoe City, outdoors, close together. Stay behind railings near the water, because the outlet is fast and cold. The area is at about 6,200 feet, so bring water and sun protection.
